tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: SubagentHandback
tools.description:
Deliver your final report to the agent that spawned you (your caller). Use it once, for that hand-off only: when your work is complete, call SubagentHandback({message: <your full report>}) as your last tool call and then stop. It is not a messaging channel: do not use it for progress updates or questions.

Only a report delivered through SubagentHandback reaches your caller; plain text you write at the end of your turn is NOT delivered. There is no recipient parameter: the report can only go to your caller.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## claude.ai Linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

## discord-setup
Discord Server Setup MCP Server

This server provides tools for automating Discord server setup using the Discord Bot API.
It can discover servers, create/manage channels, create/manage roles, configure settings, and apply templates.

Available tool categories:
- Guild: List servers, select active server, get server info
- Channels: Create/edit/delete channels and categories
- Roles: Create/edit/delete/list/reorder roles
- Settings: Configure server verification, content filter, notifications
- Templates: Apply pre-built server templates (gaming, community, business, study-group)

Role hierarchy note: Discord positions are inverted — a HIGHER position number is
higher/more powerful, @everyone is position 0 at the bottom, and newly created
roles default to the bottom. Use list_roles to see the current order, create_role
with placement:"top"/"above"/"below" to rank a role, and reorder_roles with a
top-first orderedRoleIds list rather than hand-computing position numbers.

Prerequisites:
- Discord bot created at https://discord.com/developers/applications
- Bot token configured via DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN environment variable or ~/.discord-mcp/config.json
- Bot invited to Discord server(s) with appropriate permissions (Manage Server, Manage Roles, Manage Channels)

Setup Instructions:
1. Create a Discord application at https://discord.com/developers/applications
2. Add a bot user and copy the bot token
3. Set DISCORD_BOT_TOKEN environment variable or create ~/.discord-mcp/config.json with your token
4. Generate OAuth2 URL with bot scope and required permissions
5. Invite bot to your Discord server(s)

Workflow:
1. Use list_guilds to see available servers
2. Use select_guild to set the active server
3. Use other tools to manage channels, roles, etc.

## plugin:context7:context7
Use this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service — even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. This includes API syntax, configuration, version migration, library-specific debugging, setup instructions, and CLI tool usage. ## workos
This server manages the caller's WorkOS workspace: organizations, users, SSO connections, directories, webhooks, branding, feature flags, and more. Call list_operations once to discover operations, then run them with query (reads) or mutate (writes). whoami reports the caller's identity, role, and available environment IDs. An admin may disable mutations or this server entirely for a team; the tool response says so.

This server is a control plane for an existing workspace, not a knowledge base. For WorkOS product, integration, SDK, or tooling questions, don't guess from training data or probe package registries: read https://workos.com/docs. When integrating WorkOS into a codebase, prefer the WorkOS agent skills, which carry the deep integration guides: npx skills add workos/skills

Facts agents often guess wrong: the official WorkOS CLI is the unscoped npm package "workos" (repo github.com/workos/cli). Discord Server Setup MCP Server

This server provides tools for automating Discord server setup using the Discord Bot API.
It can discover servers, create/manage channels, create/manage roles, configure settings, and apply templates.

- Roles: Create/edit/delete/list/reorder roles
- Settings: Configure server verification, content filter, notifications

1	/**
     2	 * The decks we lay a profile out for, and the keys every profile opens with.
     3	 *
     4	 * Data only: `profiles.mjs` does the arranging. Splitting them is what lets
     5	 * the test hold a layout against a grid without running a generator, and it
     6	 * keeps the one thing a person is likely to edit - what sits where - in a
     7	 * file with no machinery in it.
     8	 */
     9	
    10	/**
    11	 * The four decks, with the numbers a layout needs.
    12	 *
    13	 * `model` is the string the Stream Deck app writes into a profile's
    14	 * `Device.Model`, taken from the app's own shipped profiles rather than
    15	 * guessed: `DefaultProfiles/StreamDeck*_winDefault.streamDeckProfile` for the
    16	 * Stream Deck, the Mini and the +, and the XL from a plugin that ships one.
    17	 * `type` is the manifest's `DeviceType`, which is the SDK's own enumeration.
    18	 *
    19	 * A + has eight keys and four dials, and they are two different controllers
    20	 * in a profile rather than twelve positions on one.
    21	 */
    22	export const DEVICES = {
    23	  xl: { model: "20GAT9901", type: 2, columns: 8, rows: 4, dials: 0 },
    24	  sd: { model: "20GAA9902", type: 0, columns: 5, rows: 3, dials: 0 },
    25	  mini: { model: "20GAI9901", type: 1, columns: 3, rows: 2, dials: 0 },
    26	  plus: { model: "20GBD9901", type: 7, columns: 4, rows: 2, dials: 4 },
    27	};
    28	
    29	/**
    30	 * The keys every profile opens with, in the order they are laid down.
    31	 *
    32	 * Connect first because nothing else does anything until it has been
    33	 * pressed, then the run it is on, then the three presses somebody reaches
    34	 * for mid-scene, then the numbers. The dedicated Roll key and the Press key
    35	 * set to the waiting roll are both here on purpose: Roll is lit only while
    36	 * dice are waiting, and Press takes the primary whatever it is, so the two
    37	 * say different things about the same moment.
    38	 *
    39	 * The clock and the dice the run throws for itself sit with the presses,
    40	 * because both are things somebody reaches for while a scene is running.
    41	 *
    42	 * The two Open keys come last but one because nothing on the deck needs
    43	 * them mid-scene: one puts the run in the browser, the other the guide.
    44	 * Finish is last of all, as far from a hand mid-scene as the layout goes,
    45	 * and it takes a hold on top of that.
    46	 *
    47	 * Fourteen keys, which is more than a Mini or a + has room for. They page.
    48	 */
    49	export const BASE = [
    50	  { action: "connect" },
    51	  { action: "run" },
    52	  { action: "next" },
    53	  { action: "roll" },
    54	  { action: "undo" },
    55	  { action: "clock" },
    56	  { action: "autoroll" },
    57	  { action: "metric", settings: { field: "score" } },
    58	  { action: "metric", settings: { field: "unit" } },
    59	  { action: "metric", settings: { field: "clock" } },
    60	  { action: "press", settings: { target: { kind: "roll" } } },
    61	  { action: "open", settings: { target: "run" } },
    62	  { action: "open", settings: { target: "guide" } },
    63	  { action: "finish" },
    64	];
    65	
    66	/**
    67	 * What the four dials on a + carry.
    68	 *
    69	 * Next, Metric and Clock declare `Encoder` in the manifest, so those three
    70	 * are what can sit here at all. They repeat on every page of a + profile:
    71	 * paging moves the keys, and a clock you can no longer see because you
    72	 * turned to the moves is a dial doing nobody any good. The clock is the
    73	 * action rather than the metric's readout of it, so turning to it and
    74	 * pressing the dial pauses or resumes rather than doing nothing.
    75	 */
    76	export const DIALS = [
    77	  { action: "next" },
    78	  { action: "metric", settings: { field: "score" } },
    79	  { action: "clock" },
    80	  { action: "metric", settings: { field: "unit" } },
    81	];
    82	
    83	/**
    84	 * The packs a profile is laid out for: the demo pack, and every sketch.
    85	 *
    86	 * Paths rather than a list of packs, because the list is whatever is on
    87	 * disk. `profiles.mjs` reads the sketches folder, so a pack added to the
    88	 * repository has a profile on the next run of the generator without anybody
    89	 * editing a list here.
    90	 */
    91	export const DEMO = { slug: "demo", file: "packs/demo/pack.yaml" };
    92	export const SKETCHES = "packs/sketches";
    93	
    94	/**
    95	 * A pack's slug is its file's stem, and these are the exceptions.
    96	 *
    97	 * The slug is what names the `.streamDeckProfile` file, the manifest entry
    98	 * and the profile the plugin switches to, so changing one renames a profile
    99	 * on every deck that already has it. Elden Ring's was laid out before the
   100	 * rule existed and keeps the name it shipped under.
   101	 */
   102	export const SLUGS = { "elden-ring-tarnishedtool": "elden-ring" };
   103	
   104	/**
   105	 * A setup a pack's profile puts on a Command key rather than an Apply-setup one.
   106	 *
   107	 * A setup that moves the player is a different kind of press from one that
   108	 * only changes what they are holding: it happens once, it does not touch
   109	 * the run's own setup, and it is worth a key that says so rather than one
   110	 * that says "Apply setup" about a warp. `Warp` at the front of the title is
   111	 * how an author says so on purpose; a `warp.*` op is how the tool says so
   112	 * whether the author thought to name it that or not.
   113	 */
   114	export function isWarp(setup) {
   115	  return setup.title.startsWith("Warp") || (setup.ops ?? []).some((op) => op.op.startsWith("warp."));
   116	}

content.content: 5:Profiles come with it, laid out for each deck (Stream Deck, Mini, XL and +). The Runlog profile installs with the plugin. A pack's profile has that pack's moves on keys, its counters and resources on the numbers, and its setups ready to hand out; it arrives the first time your deck follows a run of that pack, and the deck switches to it. **Switch to the pack's profile when a run attaches**, in Connect's settings, turns that off. A pack Runlog ships no profile for, one you bought or wrote yourself, puts the deck on the Runlog profile. Once a profile is yours you can rearrange it like any other.

/**
 * A Stream Deck profile built from a pack, in Node or in a browser.
 *
 * `streamdeck/design/profiles.mjs` runs this over the packs in the
 * repository and commits the forty-four files the plugin ships. A pack
 * from the Marketplace is not known when the plugin is packed, so its own
 * page runs the same code on the pack it is showing and hands over the
 * bytes. Nothing here touches the filesystem or a Node built-in, which is
 * what lets both callers be the same code rather than two that drift.
 */

export { BASE, DEVICE_IDS, DEVICES, DIALS, isWarp, type Device, type DeviceId, type Key } from "./layouts.ts";
export { ACTION_NAMES, PAGE_PLUGIN, PLUGIN, TURNS } from "./plugin.ts";
export {
  container,
  GENERIC,
  hasKeys,
  packKeys,
  paginate,
  profile,
  specs,
  stableId,
  type Built,
  type Controller,
  type Page,
  type PageFile,
  type ProfileSpec,
  type RootFile,
  type StoredAction,
} from "./profiles.ts";
export { zip, type ZipEntry } from "./zip.ts";

14	 * Nobody reads a `.streamDeckProfile`. It is a zip of compact JSON that
15	 * goes out with a release or off a pack's page and turns up on somebody's
16	 * desk, and the two ways it goes wrong, a key off the edge of a Mini and a

23	 * files committed under the plugin, byte for byte. Those are generated by
24	 * `streamdeck/design/profiles.mjs`, which is a Node script over this code;
25	 * proving the package alone reproduces them is what says a browser
26	 * building a profile for a Marketplace pack is building the same thing.

29	const repo = new URL("../../../", import.meta.url);
30	const path = (rest: string) => fileURLToPath(new URL(rest, repo));

32	/** Every setup written for a tool, by title, the way the app's picker lists them. */
33	function setupsFor(tool: string | undefined): Setup[] {
34	  if (!tool) return [];
35	  const dir = path("packs/setups");
36	  const out: Setup[] = [];
37	  for (const file of readdirSync(dir).filter((f) => f.endsWith(".yaml"))) {
38	    const parsed = loadSetupText(readFileSync(`${dir}/${file}`, "utf8"), "yaml");
39	    if (parsed.ok && parsed.setup.tool.toLowerCase() === tool.toLowerCase()) out.push(parsed.setup);
40	  }
41	  return out.sort((a, b) => a.title.localeCompare(b.title));
42	}

44	/** The tool a pack is driven by, from the control profile written for it. */
45	function toolFor(packId: string): string | undefined {
46	  const dir = path("packs/profiles");
47	  for (const file of readdirSync(dir).filter((f) => f.endsWith(".json"))) {
48	    const written = JSON.parse(readFileSync(`${dir}/${file}`, "utf8")) as { pack?: string; tool?: string };

/**
 * The decks we lay a profile out for, and the keys every profile opens with.
 *
 * Data only: `profiles.mjs` does the arranging. Splitting them is what lets
 * the test hold a layout against a grid without running a generator, and it
 * keeps the one thing a person is likely to edit - what sits where - in a
 * file with no machinery in it.
 */

/**
 * The four decks, with the numbers a layout needs.
 *
 * `model` is the string the Stream Deck app writes into a profile's
 * `Device.Model`, taken from the app's own shipped profiles rather than
 * guessed: `DefaultProfiles/StreamDeck*_winDefault.streamDeckProfile` for the
 * Stream Deck, the Mini and the +, and the XL from a plugin that ships one.
 * `type` is the manifest's `DeviceType`, which is the SDK's own enumeration.
 *
 * A + has eight keys and four dials, and they are two different controllers
 * in a profile rather than twelve positions on one.
 */
export const DEVICES = {
  xl: { model: "20GAT9901", type: 2, columns: 8, rows: 4, dials: 0 },
  sd: { model: "20GAA9902", type: 0, columns: 5, rows: 3, dials: 0 },
  mini: { model: "20GAI9901", type: 1, columns: 3, rows: 2, dials: 0 },
  plus: { model: "20GBD9901", type: 7, columns: 4, rows: 2, dials: 4 },
};

/**
 * The keys every profile opens with, in the order they are laid down.
 *
 * Connect first because nothing else does anything until it has been
 * pressed, then the run it is on, then the three presses somebody reaches
 * for mid-scene, then the numbers. The dedicated Roll key and the Press key
 * set to the waiting roll are both here on purpose: Roll is lit only while
 * dice are waiting, and Press takes the primary whatever it is, so the two
 * say different things about the same moment.
 *
 * The clock and the dice the run throws for itself sit with the presses,
 * because both are things somebody reaches for while a scene is running.
 *
 * The two Open keys come last but one because nothing on the deck needs
 * them mid-scene: one puts the run in the browser, the other the guide.
 * Finish is last of all, as far from a hand mid-scene as the layout goes,
 * and it takes a hold on top of that.
 *
 * Fourteen keys, which is more than a Mini or a + has room for. They page.
 */
export const BASE = [
  { action: "connect" },
  { action: "run" },
  { action: "next" },
  { action: "roll" },
  { action: "undo" },
  { action: "clock" },
  { action: "autoroll" },
  { action: "metric", settings: { field: "score" } },
  { action: "metric", settings: { field: "unit" } },
  { action: "metric", settings: { field: "clock" } },
  { action: "press", settings: { target: { kind: "roll" } } },
  { action: "open", settings: { target: "run" } },
  { action: "open", settings: { target: "guide" } },
  { action: "finish" },
];

/**
 * What the four dials on a + carry.
 *
 * Next, Metric and Clock declare `Encoder` in the manifest, so those three
 * are what can sit here at all. They repeat on every page of a + profile:
 * paging moves the keys, and a clock you can no longer see because you
 * turned to the moves is a dial doing nobody any good. The clock is the
 * action rather than the metric's readout of it, so turning to it and
 * pressing the dial pauses or resumes rather than doing nothing.
 */
export const DIALS = [
  { action: "next" },
  { action: "metric", settings: { field: "score" } },
  { action: "clock" },
  { action: "metric", settings: { field: "unit" } },
];

/**
 * The packs a profile is laid out for: the demo pack, and every sketch.
 *
 * Paths rather than a list of packs, because the list is whatever is on
 * disk. `profiles.mjs` reads the sketches folder, so a pack added to the
 * repository has a profile on the next run of the generator without anybody
 * editing a list here.
 */
export const DEMO = { slug: "demo", file: "packs/demo/pack.yaml" };
export const SKETCHES = "packs/sketches";

/**
 * A pack's slug is its file's stem, and these are the exceptions.
 *
 * The slug is what names the `.streamDeckProfile` file, the manifest entry
 * and the profile the plugin switches to, so changing one renames a profile
 * on every deck that already has it. Elden Ring's was laid out before the
 * rule existed and keeps the name it shipped under.
 */
export const SLUGS = { "elden-ring-tarnishedtool": "elden-ring" };

/**
 * A setup a pack's profile puts on a Command key rather than an Apply-setup one.
 *
 * A setup that moves the player is a different kind of press from one that
 * only changes what they are holding: it happens once, it does not touch
 * the run's own setup, and it is worth a key that says so rather than one
 * that says "Apply setup" about a warp. `Warp` at the front of the title is
 * how an author says so on purpose; a `warp.*` op is how the tool says so
 * whether the author thought to name it that or not.
 */
export function isWarp(setup) {
  return setup.title.startsWith("Warp") || (setup.ops ?? []).some((op) => op.op.startsWith("warp."));
}

# A Stream Deck at the table

Runlog's plugin is in the Stream Deck Marketplace, under **Runlog**. Install it and thirteen actions appear in the action list: Connect, Run, Next action, Press, Roll, Keep rolling for me, Apply setup, Command, Undo, Metric, Clock, Finish the run, and Open in the browser. It needs the Stream Deck app at 7.1 or later.

Profiles come with it, laid out for each deck (Stream Deck, Mini, XL and +). The Runlog profile installs with the plugin. A pack's profile has that pack's moves on keys, its counters and resources on the numbers, and its setups ready to hand out; it arrives the first time your deck follows a run of that pack, and the deck switches to it. **Switch to the pack's profile when a run attaches**, in Connect's settings, turns that off. A pack Runlog ships no profile for, one you bought or wrote yourself, puts the deck on the Runlog profile. Once a profile is yours you can rearrange it like any other.

## Signing in

Every key's settings carry the same account block: the Runlog address, **Sign in**, **Sign out**, **Reconnect**, and a line saying who is signed in. Leave the address alone unless you run a copy of your own.

# A Stream Deck at the table

Runlog's plugin is in the Stream Deck Marketplace, under **Runlog**. Install it and thirteen actions appear in the action list: Connect, Run, Next action, Press, Roll, Keep rolling for me, Apply setup, Command, Undo, Metric, Clock, Finish the run, and Open in the browser. It needs the Stream Deck app at 7.1 or later.

Profiles come with it, laid out for each deck (Stream Deck, Mini, XL and +). The Runlog profile installs with the plugin. A pack's profile has that pack's moves on keys, its counters and resources on the numbers, and its setups ready to hand out; it arrives the first time your deck follows a run of that pack, and the deck switches to it. **Switch to the pack's profile when a run attaches**, in Connect's settings, turns that off. A pack Runlog ships no profile for, one you bought or wrote yourself, puts the deck on the Runlog profile. Once a profile is yours you can rearrange it like any other.

## Signing in

Every key's settings carry the same account block: the Runlog address, **Sign in**, **Sign out**, **Reconnect**, and a line saying who is signed in. Leave the address alone unless you run a copy of your own.

**Sign in** shows a code and a link. Open the link in a browser, type the code, and you are signed in on the deck; the plugin keeps that sign-in in a file of its own, not in the settings the pages read. Signing in is not connecting: press Connect after.

## Connect

The key says **Connect** while the connection is closed and **Disconnect** while it is open; press it either way. Nothing is open until you press it, and a connection holding no run closes itself after thirty minutes; the key then says _went idle_ beneath Connect. A deck that is following a run stays up however long the stream goes.

Every other key says **Not connected**, with _press Connect_ beneath it, while the connection is off, and **Offline** for the moment it takes to open.

## The run the deck is on

The deck presses through the page that holds the run, so it only ever sees a run that is synced to your account and open on a page somewhere: the app in a browser tab, a [dock](#guide/dock), or a browser source. With nothing synced the keys say **Not synced**; with runs synced but none open, **No run open**.

**Run** names the run the deck is following. Press it to cycle through the runs open to you and pin the next one; its settings list the same runs by name. A pin holds: a pinned run that ends says **That run has ended** rather than moving the deck to whichever run went next. Where one run is open and nothing is pinned, the deck follows that one; where several are open and none is pinned, the keys say **Pick a run**.

## The keys

- **Next action** presses whatever the run is waiting on: rolling the table, carrying on, closing the unit, entering the next. It carries the step's own words. Where the step waits on a checklist it ticks everything and presses the step's own button; where it waits on a name, it takes the first suggestion. Tick **Stop at decisions** in its settings and it leaves both to the page.
- **Press** does the one thing you pick in its settings: a move the pack offers, the roll that is waiting, or a preset answer.
- **Roll** throws the dice the run is waiting on. It needs no settings, and is lit only while a roll is on offer.
- **Keep rolling for me** hands the dice to the run so it throws them itself; press it again to take them back. The key says which of the two the run is on.
- **Apply setup** changes the run's loadout to a setup from your library and hands it out to the tool, set in its settings. The list is your library for the pack's tool; a tool has to be attached to the run for the hand-out to reach it.
- **Command** sends a setup's operations to the tool once, without changing the run's own setup. A warp is the usual one: it moves the player without swapping what the run is holding them to.
- **Undo** takes back the last result. It is lit when there is something to take back and dim when there is not.
- **Metric** shows one number and nothing else: the score, the unit, a clock, the last result, the leader, or a counter or resource the pack keeps. Set to a counter or a resource it is a key as well: a press steps it up by one, or puts it at a number, picked under **On press** in its settings; holding it takes one back off. The other five are the run's own arithmetic and take no press.
- **Clock** counts the run's clock down on the key. Press it to pause the clock, press again to resume, and hold it to stop the clock for good. It says **No clock** where the run keeps none.
- **Finish the run** ends the run, and carries the ending it would take. Hold it for a second and a half; a press says no, so the run does not end on a key caught in passing. It says **Not yet** while the run cannot end.
- **Open in the browser** opens one page in your default browser, picked in its settings: the run the deck is following, that run's dock, a new run, this guide, or the pack's rules. The guide opens whether or not the deck is connected.

On a Stream Deck +, Next action, Metric and Clock sit on a dial as well as a key. Turning a Metric dial steps through the score, the unit, the clock, the last result and the leader, and a running clock redraws every second. Pressing a Metric dial set to a counter or a resource steps it up by one; pressing a Clock dial pauses the clock or resumes it.

# A Stream Deck at the table

Runlog's plugin is in the Stream Deck Marketplace, under **Runlog**. Install it and thirteen actions appear in the action list: Connect, Run, Next action, Press, Roll, Keep rolling for me, Apply setup, Command, Undo, Metric, Clock, Finish the run, and Open in the browser. It needs the Stream Deck app at 7.1 or later.

Profiles come with it, laid out for each deck (Stream Deck, Mini, XL and +). The Runlog profile installs with the plugin. A pack's profile has that pack's moves on keys, its counters and resources on the numbers, and its setups ready to hand out; it arrives the first time your deck follows a run of that pack, and the deck switches to it. **Switch to the pack's profile when a run attaches**, in Connect's settings, turns that off. A pack Runlog ships no profile for, one you bought or wrote yourself, puts the deck on the Runlog profile. A pack from the Marketplace has its own profile on its page, under **Stream Deck profile**: pick your deck, and import the file the Stream Deck app. Once a profile is yours you can rearrange it like any other.

## Signing in

Every key's settings carry the same account block: the Runlog address, **Sign in**, **Sign out**, **Reconnect**, and a line saying who is signed in. Leave the address alone unless you run a copy of your own.

**Sign in** shows a code and a link. Open the link in a browser, type the code, and you are signed in on the deck; the plugin keeps that sign-in in a file of its own, not in the settings the pages read. Signing in is not connecting: press Connect after.

## Connect

The key says **Connect** while the connection is closed and **Disconnect** while it is open; press it either way. Nothing is open until you press it, and a connection holding no run closes itself after thirty minutes; the key then says _went idle_ beneath Connect. A deck that is following a run stays up however long the stream goes.

Every other key says **Not connected**, with _press Connect_ beneath it, while the connection is off, and **Offline** for the moment it takes to open.

## The run the deck is on

The deck presses through the page that holds the run, so it only ever sees a run that is synced to your account and open on a page somewhere: the app in a browser tab, a [dock](#guide/dock), or a browser source. With nothing synced the keys say **Not synced**; with runs synced but none open, **No run open**.

**Run** names the run the deck is following. Press it to cycle through the runs open to you and pin the next one; its settings list the same runs by name. A pin holds: a pinned run that ends says **That run has ended** rather than moving the deck to whichever run went next. Where one run is open and nothing is pinned, the deck follows that one; where several are open and none is pinned, the keys say **Pick a run**.

## The keys

- **Next action** presses whatever the run is waiting on: rolling the table, carrying on, closing the unit, entering the next. It carries the step's own words. Where the step waits on a checklist it ticks everything and presses the step's own button; where it waits on a name, it takes the first suggestion. Tick **Stop at decisions** in its settings and it leaves both to the page.
- **Press** does the one thing you pick in its settings: a move the pack offers, the roll that is waiting, or a preset answer.
- **Roll** throws the dice the run is waiting on. It needs no settings, and is lit only while a roll is on offer.
- **Keep rolling for me** hands the dice to the run so it throws them itself; press it again to take them back. The key says which of the two the run is on.
- **Apply setup** changes the run's loadout to a setup from your library and hands it out to the tool, set in its settings. The list is your library for the pack's tool; a tool has to be attached to the run for the hand-out to reach it.
- **Command** sends a setup's operations to the tool once, without changing the run's own setup. A warp is the usual one: it moves the player without swapping what the run is holding them to.
- **Undo** takes back the last result. It is lit when there is something to take back and dim when there is not.
- **Metric** shows one number and nothing else: the score, the unit, a clock, the last result, the leader, or a counter or resource the pack keeps. Set to a counter or a resource it is a key as well: a press steps it up by one, or puts it at a number, picked under **On press** in its settings; holding it takes one back off. The other five are the run's own arithmetic and take no press.
- **Clock** counts the run's clock down on the key. Press it to pause the clock, press again to resume, and hold it to stop the clock for good. It says **No clock** where the run keeps none.
- **Finish the run** ends the run, and carries the ending it would take. Hold it for a second and a half; a press says no, so the run does not end on a key caught in passing. It says **Not yet** while the run cannot end.
- **Open in the browser** opens one page in your default browser, picked in its settings: the run the deck is following, that run's dock, a new run, this guide, or the pack's rules. The guide opens whether or not the deck is connected.

On a Stream Deck +, Next action, Metric and Clock sit on a dial as well as a key. Turning a Metric dial steps through the score, the unit, the clock, the last result and the leader, and a running clock redraws every second. Pressing a Metric dial set to a counter or a resource steps it up by one; pressing a Clock dial pauses the clock or resumes it.

A press the run has moved past, or one the page has to take, comes back refused: the key says why for three seconds, then goes back to what it was saying.

## Keeping the page awake

Chrome discards tabs it thinks nobody is looking at, and a discarded tab is a run the deck can no longer see. Keep the run in an OBS dock or a browser source, or exempt Runlog from Memory Saver in the browser's settings.

<Note>
  Where plans are switched on, pressing a run from a deck is part of Plus. Watching one (the run's name and its numbers on your keys) is
  not.
</Note>

# Task 32 report: a Stream Deck profile for any pack, downloaded from its page

Status: done. Branch `a-profile-from-the-page`, two commits, nothing pushed.

- `26c9319` refactor(deck): the profile generator is a package the browser can run
- `3e9deae` feat(marketplace): a stream deck profile for any pack, from its page

## What was built

### `packages/deck-profiles` (`@runlog/deck-profiles`, private, ESM TS)

The pure core lifted out of `streamdeck/design/profiles.mjs` and `layouts.mjs`. No Node built-ins in
the source; only the tests read files.

- `src/sha1.ts`: a hand-written SHA-1 over `Uint8Array`, plus `utf8` and `joined`. Version 5 UUIDs are
  SHA-1 by definition, `node:crypto` is not in a browser and `crypto.subtle.digest` is async, so the
  digest is written out to keep the whole generator synchronous on both sides.
- `src/layouts.ts`: `DEVICES` (now carrying a `label`: XL, Stream Deck, Mini, +), `DEVICE_IDS`, `BASE`,
  `DIALS`, `isWarp`.
- `src/plugin.ts`: `PLUGIN`, `ACTION_NAMES`, `PAGE_PLUGIN`, `TURNS`. These used to be read out of the
  plugin manifest with `node:fs`; a browser has no manifest to read, so they are constants guarded by
  `src/plugin.test.ts`, which holds them against
  `streamdeck/com.scrthq.runlog.sdPlugin/manifest.json`.
- `src/zip.ts`: the store-only zip writer, in bytes rather than Buffers. Returns `Uint8Array`.
- `src/profiles.ts`: `stableId`, `packKeys`, `hasKeys`, `paginate`, `profile(spec, ids?)`,
  `container(built)`, `specs(pack, setups, device?)`. `specs` returns one spec per deck (or just the
  deck named); a pack's slug defaults to its id, which is what a download from a pack's page is named
  after.

Tests moved with it. `src/profiles.test.ts` reads the packs, the shipped control profiles and the
setups from the repository, maps each pack to the slug it ships under through the committed
`streamdeck/src/profiles.ts` table, and asserts the package rebuilds all 44 committed
`.streamDeckProfile` files byte for byte, alongside the grid, pagination, settings-shape, dial and
per-pack content checks.

### The Node script

`streamdeck/design/profiles.mjs` is now a thin script over the package: it reads the packs, works out
each pack's tool and setups, puts the shipped slug on each spec, writes the files and
`streamdeck/src/profiles.ts`, and checks the manifest still lists what it wrote. `design/layouts.mjs`
keeps only the repository facts (`DEMO`, `SKETCHES`, `SLUGS`). `design/profiles.test.mjs` keeps the
manifest, table, naming and byte-for-byte file checks.

`npm run profiles -w streamdeck` leaves `git status` clean: the generated bytes did not move.

### Wiring

- `vitest.config.ts` and `apps/web/vite.config.ts`: alias for `@runlog/deck-profiles`.
- `streamdeck/rollup.config.mjs`: added to the typescript plugin's `include`, the way
  `packages/session` is.
- Workspace dependency declared in `apps/web/package.json` and `streamdeck/package.json`; root
  `typecheck` gained the package's tsconfig; lockfile updated with
  `npm install --package-lock-only --ignore-scripts`.

### App

`apps/web/src/library/DeckProfiles.tsx`, mounted on every free marketplace card in
`MarketplaceView.tsx`. It is a `rowMenu` `<details>` (the pattern `PackServers.tsx` next to it uses)
labelled "Stream Deck profile". Opening it reads the pack's text; a pack that does not parse, or one
with no moves, counters or resources, removes the row. Otherwise it shows one button per deck, and a
press builds the profile from the pack plus `forTool(await setupsHere(), tool)`, where the tool comes
from the shipped control profile written for the pack, and hands the bytes over as a
`.streamDeckProfile` blob download.

The pack is read on open rather than on render on purpose: a marketplace listing's text comes over the
network, and fetching every listed pack to decide whether to draw a row nobody asked for is a page
paying for what it does not use. This is the one place the brief's wording was not followed literally
("shown only when the pack has at least one move, counter or resource"): the row is drawn, and removes
itself once the pack is known to have nothing to lay out.

Styles: a `.deckProfiles` block in `apps/web/src/styles.css`.

Guide: `apps/web/src/guide/pages/stream-deck.mdx` gained one sentence in the profiles paragraph.

## Checks

All green:

- `npx vitest run packages/deck-profiles streamdeck apps/web/src/library apps/web/src/guide --no-file-parallelism`: 35 files, 290 tests.
- `npx vitest run --no-file-parallelism` (whole suite): 175 files, 1569 tests.
- `npm run typecheck`, `npm run lint:docs`, `npm run format:check`.
- `npm run build -w streamdeck`, and `npm run build -w apps/web` for good measure.
- `npm run profiles -w streamdeck`, `git status` clean afterwards.

## Concerns

- **A junction was created by hand.** `npm install --package-lock-only` updates the lockfile but does
  not link a new workspace into `node_modules`, and without the link neither `tsc` nor
  `node design/profiles.mjs` resolves `@runlog/deck-profiles`. I created
  `node_modules/@runlog/deck-profiles` as a directory junction to `packages/deck-profiles`. A plain
  `npm install` (or CI's install) makes the same link, so nothing is committed for it, but anyone
  else picking this branch up has to install before the checks pass.
- **The plugin identity is now written in two places.** `packages/deck-profiles/src/plugin.ts` copies
  the plugin's name, UUID, version and action labels out of the plugin manifest. `plugin.test.ts`
  fails the moment they disagree, so the drift is caught, but bumping the manifest version is now a
  two-file change followed by regenerating the profiles. The alternative was importing the 13 KB
  manifest into the web bundle.
- **`@rollup/plugin-typescript TS5096` warning** on `npm run build -w streamdeck`. Pre-existing:
  `allowImportingTsExtensions` in `streamdeck/tsconfig.json` against the plugin's emitting build, and
  nothing to do with the `include` line this task touched. The build succeeds.
- **`packages/cli/src/bin.ts` turned up modified with an empty diff** early in the worktree (line
  endings only) and failed `format:check`; `git checkout --` on it restored it and it has stayed
  clean since. Not touched by this work.
- The row is offered on free listings only. A priced listing has no text to read until it is bought,
  so there is nothing to build a profile from on its card.
